extracted.intended_audience: graduate students (or advanced undergraduates) studying functional analysis / Banach space theory
extracted.subtask_description: Exercises and theorem statements from Brezis' Functional Analysis (Chapter 1 & start of Chapter 2) covering Hahn–Banach, convex conjugates, separation, Baire category, uniform boundedness, open mapping, closed graph, complements, adjoints, and related constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of normalized algebraic (Hamel) basis (using Zorn's lemma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove (using Zorn’s lemma) that there exists an algebraic basis (e_i)_{i∈I} in E such that ||e_i|| = 1 for all i ∈ I. (Recall: a Hamel basis is a subset such that every x ∈ E may be written uniquely as finite linear combination of basis elements.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Zorn’s lemma to produce a maximal linearly independent set and then normalize vectors to norm 1. The exercise appears with two follow-on items: construct a discontinuous linear functional on E, and — assuming E is Banach — prove I is uncountable (hint: Baire category theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct a discontinuous linear functional
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a linear functional f : E → R that is not continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine with the existence of a Hamel basis: define f by specifying values on basis elements so that it is unbounded on the unit ball. Use the normalized basis to make the construction explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncountability of Hamel basis in infinite-dimensional Banach spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming E is a Banach space, prove that the index set I of any Hamel basis is not countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Baire category theorem (Theorem 2.1) as hinted: a countable Hamel basis would make the space a countable union of finite-dimensional subspaces, contradicting Baire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine subspace containing a hyperplane: dichotomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Let E be a n.v.s. and H ⊂ E a hyperplane. Let V ⊂ E be an affine subspace containing H. Prove that either V = H or V = E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the defining codimension-1 property of a hyperplane: any affine superset either equals the hyperplane or spans whole space when extended by one dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperplane closed or dense
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduce that a hyperplane H in a n.v.s. is either closed or dense in E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply previous dichotomy to the closure of H: if closure strictly contains H, the affine subspace generated leads to E, so H dense; otherwise H closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convex set and interior convexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Let C ⊂ E be convex. Prove that C and Int C are convex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Straightforward verification: convexity preserved under convex combinations; show interior stable under convex combinations with an interior point (see next part).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interior point plus convex combination stays interior
rubrics_metrics.description: Given x ∈ C and y ∈ Int C, show that t x + (1 − t) y ∈ Int C for all t ∈ (0,1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use local openness around y and convexity to place a neighborhood around the convex combination inside C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convex set with nonempty interior equals its interior
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduce that C = Int C whenever Int C ≠ ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because any boundary point can be written as convex combination with interior point producing interior neighborhoods; in finite-dimensional context this is classical, but argument given above applies in n.v.s. with the interior nonempty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gauge of symmetric bounded open convex set is a norm equivalent to original
rubrics_metrics.description: Let C be open, convex, 0 ∈ C, symmetric (−C = C) and bounded in a normed space (E, ||·||). Let p be the gauge of C. Prove p is a norm equivalent to ||·||.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show p satisfies norms axioms (positivity, homogeneity, triangle inequality) using symmetry and convexity; boundedness and 0∈C yield equivalence with original norm via bounds linking sets {p≤1} and ball of ||·||.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: gauge on C([0,1]) defined by L2-ball
rubrics_metrics.description: Let E = C([0,1];R) with sup norm. Let C = {u ∈ E; ∫_0^1 |u(t)|^2 dt < 1}. Check C convex, symmetric, 0∈C. Is C bounded in E? Compute gauge p of C and show p is a norm on E. Is p equivalent to sup norm?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C is convex and symmetric but not bounded for sup-norm (functions can peak on small intervals while keeping L2 small). Compute gauge via scaling to reach L2-ball; show p defines a norm but it is not equivalent to sup norm (no uniform control over sup by L2 scaling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-dimensional separation: hyperplane separating convex set and origin
rubrics_metrics.description: In finite-dimensional normed space E, let C ⊂ E be nonempty convex with 0 ∉ C. Prove there exists a hyperplane separating C and {0}. (No additional assumptions on C required.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct countable dense subset (x_n) in C, define compact convex sets C_n = conv{x1,...,xn}, show ∪C_n is dense in C. For each n produce f_n ∈ E* with ||f_n||=1 and f_n(x) ≥ 0 for x ∈ C_n; pass to limit to obtain f separating C and 0. Use compactness of C_n and finite dimensional Hahn–Banach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of two disjoint nonempty convex sets in finite dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Let A, B ⊂ E be nonempty disjoint convex sets in finite-dimensional E. Prove existence of a hyperplane H that separates A and B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to separation from origin by translating sets, or use Minkowski functional constructions and finite-dimensional Hahn–Banach arguments (or apply previous result to convex hulls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of existence of linear functional with prescribed values (general index set)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fix (x_i)_{i∈I} in E and scalars (α_i)_{i∈I}. Show equivalence between (A) existence of f ∈ E* with f(x_i)=α_i ∀i∈I and (B) existence of M≥0 such that for every finite J⊂I and reals (β_i)_{i∈J} we have |∑_{i∈J} β_i α_i| ≤ M ||∑_{i∈J} β_i x_i||.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The implication (A)⇒(B) is immediate from boundedness of f. For (B)⇒(A) define f first on span{x_i} via the linear constraints and use Hahn–Banach to extend to E with controlled norm ≤ M. Hint: start defining on finite linear combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate solvability with bounded norm equivalent condition (finite functionals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let M>0, choose n functionals f_i ∈ E*, scalars α_i. Prove equivalence between: (A) For all ε>0 there exists x_ε ∈ E with ||x_ε|| ≤ M + ε and f_i(x_ε)=α_i ∀i; and (B) For all β_1,...,β_n ∈ R, ∑ β_i α_i ≤ M ||∑ β_i f_i|| (dual inequality form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mimic finite-dimensional Hahn–Banach arguments; if f_i are linearly independent reduce to span and use Lemma 3.3 pattern. Use dual norm bounds; (B)⇒(A) via constructing approximate solutions and Hahn–Banach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solvability of linear system of functionals on a vector space
rubrics_metrics.description: Let E be a vector space and linear functionals f_i and scalars α_i. Prove that there exists x ∈ E with f_i(x)=α_i ∀i iff for any real β_i with ∑ β_i f_i = 0 one has ∑ β_i α_i = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the classical consistency condition: necessary direction by applying linear relation to x; conversely define linear map R^n → R by β ↦ ∑ β_i α_i and use linear algebra arguments to produce x when constraints satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation in R^n of a subspace avoiding the positive orthant
rubrics_metrics.description: Let P = {x ∈ R^n; x_i ≥ 0 ∀i}. If M ⊂ R^n is a linear subspace with M ∩ P = {0}, prove there is a hyperplane H with M ⊂ H and H ∩ P = {0}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use orthogonality and interior of P; prove M⊥ ∩ Int P ≠ ∅ first (hint in text). Then deduce existence of separating functional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples in sequence spaces showing non-closed sums and separation issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Let E = ℓ^1 and define closed subspaces X and Y (specified coordinate constraints). Check X and Y are closed linear spaces and that X + Y = E; find a vector c ∉ X + Y; set Z = X − c and check Y ∩ Z = ∅; decide if there exists a closed hyperplane separating Y and Z; compare with Theorem 1.7. Repeat for ℓ^p (1<p<∞) and c_0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exercise exhibits pathologies in infinite dimensions: closed subspaces with sum not closed and separation failing. Compute direct coordinate constructions and think of dual descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bipolar/polar identity for convex sets containing 0
rubrics_metrics.description: Given C ⊂ E convex with 0∈C, define C* = {f ∈ E*; f(x) ≤ 1 ∀x ∈ C} and C** = {x ∈ E; f(x) ≤ 1 ∀f ∈ C*}. Prove C** = C. Determine C* if C is a linear space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the bipolar theorem for convex balanced sets containing 0. Use Hahn–Banach separation to show equality; when C is a linear space, polar is its annihilator scaled appropriately (compute explicitly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Annihilator and double annihilator counterexample in ℓ^1 / ℓ^∞
rubrics_metrics.description: Let E = ℓ^1 so E* = ℓ^∞. Take N = c_0 as a closed subspace of E*. Determine N^⊥ = {x ∈ E; f(x)=0 ∀f ∈ N} and N^⊥⊥ = {f ∈ E*; f(x)=0 ∀x ∈ N^⊥}. Check that N^⊥⊥ ≠ N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute annihilators explicitly using standard duality ℓ^1–ℓ^∞; c_0's annihilator leads to certain coordinate constraints. This shows double annihilator may strictly contain original subspace in non-reflexive settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonal complement of hyperplane and distance formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f ∈ E*, f ≠ 0, and M = {x; f(x)=0} the hyperplane. (1) Determine M^⊥. (2) Prove for every x ∈ E that dist(x,M) = |f(x)| / ||f||. (3) For E = {u ∈ C([0,1]): u(0)=0} with f(u)=∫_0^1 u(t) dt show dist(u,M) = |∫_0^1 u| and that the infimum is never achieved for u ∈ E  ackslash M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute M^⊥ = span{f} (suitably identified in dual). Use Hahn–Banach and norm duality to get distance formula. For the function space example, show approximating sequences exist but no minimizer because no function in E attains certain average with zero at 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute convex, l.s.c. functions and their conjugates (many examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check that various functions φ: R → (−∞,+∞] (listed (a)-(l): affine, exponential, indicator-type, −log, quadratic, p-power, hinge, etc.) are convex l.s.c. and determine their conjugate functions φ*. Draw graphs and mark epigraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each listed φ compute Legendre–Fenchel conjugate using definition φ*(s)=sup_{x}(sx − φ(x)). Consider domain constraints and indicator functions; sketch epigraphs to understand l.s.c./convexity. Several standard conjugates appear (e.g., quadratic ↔ quadratic, indicator ↔ support function).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity of conjugation and radial composition conjugate formula
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. If ϕ ≤ ψ then prove ϕ* ≥ ψ*. 2. Let F: R → (−∞,+∞] convex l.s.c. with F(0)=0 and F(t) ≥ 0. Set ϕ(x)=F(||x||). Prove ϕ convex l.s.c. and ϕ*(f) = F*(||f||) for f in E*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conjugation definition and change of variables to establish monotonicity; for radial composition use rotational invariance and dual norm relationship to reduce conjugation to scalar radial conjugation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugates in ℓ^p spaces (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let E = ℓ^p, 1 ≤ p < ∞. For several functions ϕ on E defined by weighted sums or constraints, check convexity, l.s.c., and determine ϕ*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply standard duality between ℓ^p and ℓ^q (1/p + 1/q =1), compute suprema componentwise; ensure domain conditions for finiteness are checked. Examples include weighted ℓ^2-type sums or growth conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convexity and conjugate of φ(x)=√(x1 x2) on positive quadrant
rubrics_metrics.description: On E = R^2 let φ(x) = √(x1 x2) if x in C = {x1,x2 ≥ 0}, +∞ otherwise. (1) Prove φ convex l.s.c. (2) Determine φ*. (3) With D the set {x1=0} and ψ = I_D compute inf_x {φ(x)+ψ(x)} and sup_{f∈E*}{−φ*(−f) − ψ*(f)} and compare to Theorem 1.12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This examines Fenchel duality and cases where hypotheses of Theorem 1.12 fail (lack of interior point in domain intersection). Compute explicit formulas using homogeneity and support functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance to closed set: convexity and conjugate decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Let A ⊂ E be closed nonempty and define ϕ(x)=dist(x,A). (1) Prove Lipschitz: |ϕ(x)−ϕ(y)| ≤ ||x−y||. (2) If A convex, show ϕ convex. (3) Conversely, if ϕ convex then A convex. (4) Prove ϕ* = (I_A)^* + I_{B_E}^* (explicit relation between conjugates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use basic properties of infimum over closed sets for Lipschitz and convexity; for conjugate identity follow from definition and separation arguments (exercise references Theorem 1.12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inf-convolution: definition and basic properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Define (ϕ ⨅ ψ)(x) = inf_{y∈E} {ϕ(x−y) + ψ(y)}. Prove: (i) values may be ±∞; (ii) finite iff x ∈ D(ϕ)+D(ψ); (iii) conjugacy relations e.g., (ϕ+ψ)^* ≤ (ϕ^* ⨅ ψ^*), and under conditions equality holds; (iv) epigraph relation epigraph(ϕ ⨅ ψ) = epigraph ϕ + epigraph ψ when domains intersect; deduce convexity when ϕ,ψ convex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work through stated subparts: avoid −∞ by domain assumptions; use epigraph geometry to deduce convexity and conjugacy equalities under continuity at some point or interior-point hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularization by inf-convolution (Moreau envelope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given convex l.s.c. ϕ not identically +∞, define ϕ_n(x) = inf_y { n ||x−y|| + ϕ(y) }. Prove existence of N so ϕ_n finite for n≥N; each ϕ_n convex continuous (Lipschitz with constant n); compute (ϕ_n)^*; show ϕ_n ≤ ϕ and ϕ_n(x) increases to ϕ(x) for x ∈ D(ϕ) and →+∞ outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard Moreau–Yosida regularization: show finiteness by approximation, Lipschitz from n||·|| term, monotone convergence by choosing minimizing sequences and showing limit behavior using density and coercivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semiscalar product and representation via duality map
rubrics_metrics.description: Define [x,y] = inf_{t>0} (ϕ(x+ty) − ϕ(x))/t for appropriate ϕ; in particular define [x,y] = inf_{t>0} (1/(2t))(||x+ty||^2 − ||x||^2). Prove monotonicity of h(t), bound |[x,y]| ≤ ||x|| ||y||, partial bilinearity under sign restrictions, convexity of y ↦ [x,y], l.s.c. of G(x,y)=−[x,y], and representation [x,y] = max_{f ∈ F(x)} f(y) where F is the duality map. Determine explicit formula in R^n with p-norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use calculus-like expansions of norms, convexity of squared norm, and duality mapping properties. For explicit formula use conjugate or Holder computations in ℓ^p norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict convexity for norms and functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Define strictly convex norm and strictly convex function. Prove: norm ||·|| strictly convex iff ϕ(x)=||x||^2 strictly convex. Same question for ϕ(x)=||x||^p with 1<p<∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the characterization via strict inequality on unit sphere and homogeneity properties. For p-norms use convexity properties of |·|^p and Clarkson-type inequalities if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonextendability of continuous linear maps from non-complemented subspace
rubrics_metrics.description: Let E Banach and G ⊂ E closed subspace that admits no complement. Let F = G and T = identity on G. Prove T cannot be extended by a continuous linear map T : E → F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If extension existed it would provide a continuous projection from E onto G (compose extension with inclusion), contradicting that G has no continuous complement. Compare with Corollary 1.2 conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baire Category Theorem (Theorem 2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X be a complete metric space and (X_n) sequence of closed subsets with ∪_n X_n = X. Then some X_{n0} has nonempty interior. Equivalently, countable intersection of dense open sets is dense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard proof by constructing nested balls; frequently used to deduce generic (comeagre) properties and in functional analysis results like uniform boundedness and open mapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform Boundedness Principle (Banach–Steinhaus, Theorem 2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let E,F Banach, (T_i) family of continuous linear operators E→F. If for every x ∈ E, sup_i ||T_i x|| < ∞ (pointwise boundedness), then sup_i ||T_i||_{L(E,F)} < ∞ (uniform boundedness). Equivalently, ∃c with ||T_i x|| ≤ c ||x|| for all i,x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Baire category applied to sets X_n = {x: sup_i ||T_i x|| ≤ n}. Remark: linearity is essential; pointwise limit of continuous linear maps need not converge in operator norm. Corollaries include boundedness of sup_n ||T_n|| for pointwise convergent sequences and weak⇔strong boundedness results for sets seen through duals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries of uniform boundedness: sequences and boundedness via functionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary 2.3: If (T_n) continuous operators with T_n x converging pointwise to T x, then sup_n ||T_n|| < ∞, T ∈ L(E,F), and ||T|| ≤ liminf ||T_n||. Corollary 2.4/2.5: boundedness of set B in Banach space G follows from boundedness of all evaluations f(B) for f∈G* (weakly bounded ⇒ strongly bounded), and dual statement for subsets of G*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Theorem 2.2 to appropriate families of operators (evaluation maps). These are standard consequences used to pass from pointwise bounds to uniform operator bounds or norm bounds on sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open Mapping Theorem (Theorem 2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If T: E→F is a surjective continuous linear map between Banach spaces then T maps open sets to open sets; concretely ∃c>0 such that T(B_E(0,1)) ⊃ B_F(0,c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Baire category on nT(B(0,1)). Consequences: inverse of bijective continuous linear map is continuous (Corollary 2.7) and equivalence of norms when both complete and one inequality holds (Corollary 2.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed Graph Theorem (Theorem 2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If T : E→F is linear between Banach spaces and its graph G(T) is closed in E×F, then T is continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: equip E with the graph norm ||x||_1 = ||x||_E + ||T x||_F. Closedness of graph ⇒ (E,||·||_1) complete. Compare norms ||·||_1 and ||·||_2 = ||·||_E (second complete). Use equivalence of norms to deduce continuity of T.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementary subspaces and bounded decompositions (Theorem 2.10 & Corollary 2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: If G and L are closed subspaces of Banach space E with G+L closed, then every z ∈ G+L can be decomposed z = x+y with x∈G,y∈L and norms controlled: ||x||,||y|| ≤ C||z|| for some C. Consequently dist(x,G∩L) ≤ C(dist(x,G)+dist(x,L)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses open mapping theorem applied to map T: G×L → G+L, T(x,y)=x+y. Corollary gives stability of projections and a criterion for closedness of G+L. Remarks: existence of complements equivalent to bounded projections; finite-dimensional or finite-codimension cases always admit complements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right and left inverses equivalences for bounded operators (Theorems 2.12 & 2.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 2.12: For surjective T∈L(E,F), T admits right inverse ⇔ N(T) admits a complement in E. Theorem 2.13: For injective T, T admits left inverse ⇔ R(T) is closed and admits a complement in F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct inverses explicitly from complements and projections. Remarks: existence of closed subspaces without complement implies existence of surjective operators without right inverse (canonical quotient map example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonality relations for closed subspaces (Proposition 2.14, Corollary 2.15, Theorem 2.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulas: G∩L = (G^⊥ + L^⊥)^⊥ and G^⊥ ∩ L^⊥ = (G+L)^⊥. Equivalences: G+L closed ⇔ G^⊥ + L^⊥ closed ⇔ G+L = (G^⊥ ∩ L^⊥)^⊥ ⇔ G^⊥ + L^⊥ = (G∩L)^⊥.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use basic orthogonality inclusions and Hahn–Banach to prove equalities; proofs use duality representations of distances and Theorem 2.10/2.11 to pass closedness between sums and sums of annihilators. Theorem 2.16 gives multiple equivalent characterizations linking closedness and orthogonal sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and basic facts about unbounded linear operators and adjoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Define unbounded linear operator A: D(A)⊂E→F (domain D(A) linear). Graph, range, kernel and closedness notion. If A densely defined, define adjoint A^* with domain D(A^*) = {v∈F^*; ∃c≥0 s.t. |⟨v,Au⟩| ≤ c||u|| ∀u∈D(A)} and A^*v the extension of u↦⟨v,Au⟩ to E via Hahn–Banach / density.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: closed A ⇒ N(A) closed, but R(A) need not be closed. If A bounded then A^* bounded and ||A^*|| = ||A||. Construction of adjoint uses boundedness on dense domain and extension by continuity; domain of A^* may not be dense in general but is dense for weak-* topology and in reflexive case dense in norm.
